fit_paragraph: This year's priority, international and open economy macroeconomics and international finance, is where both of my papers meet. My job market paper separates the response of inflation to a sector's own labor shortages from the response to shortages shared across economies; for an open economy like the UK, that is the question of how much inflationary pressure is domestic and how much comes from abroad, and the Bank's Agents and Decision Maker Panel collect the kind of firm-level evidence the method is built for. The convenience yield paper measures how one sovereign's debt supply moves the price of safety for others, a question that extends to gilts alongside Bunds and Treasuries, and my work on Eurosystem collateral eligibility speaks to the design of a central bank's collateral framework. I would bring this agenda to the Bank's research on global spillovers and present it to policymakers as well as to academic audiences.

fit_paragraph: GW's macroeconomists work on the two questions my research asks, with the Federal Reserve Board, the IMF and the Treasury a short walk from campus. Tara Sinclair's work on real-time economic analysis and forecasting is close to the practical use of my job market paper, which shows that inflation responds far more to labor shortages shared across the economy than to local ones and so changes how survey evidence on tightness should be read. Graciela Kaminsky's research in international finance and open-economy macroeconomics is the natural audience for the convenience yield paper, which measures how one sovereign's debt supply moves the price of safety for others. I would be glad to teach core and specialized courses in macroeconomics and international finance at the undergraduate and graduate level.

institution: MIT FutureTech (MIT Sloan IDE and CSAIL)
fit_paragraph: Of FutureTech's four project areas, the labor market effects of AI and the effect of AI on science and growth are the two I would most like to work on, and both connect to my research. AI is a common shock whose reach differs sharply across occupations, firms and sectors, which is the setting in which my job market paper shows that standard cross-sectional designs confound a unit's own exposure with the shock it shares with the rest of the economy; the two-step method I develop to separate the two carries over to estimating how AI exposure moves wages and employment. My project with Boris Hofmann finds that, across 130 years and 17 advanced economies, faster productivity growth has come with lower inflation and unchanged long-term nominal rates, a historical benchmark for the macroeconomic consequences of AI-driven growth. I would welcome the chance to work in Neil Thompson's interdisciplinary team and to mentor the students in it.
